claim: A three-stage pipeline (LLM extraction with supporting quotes, embedding-based semantic mapping to a taxonomy, and LLM-as-a-judge validation) extracts 10,688 structured risk factors from S&P 500 10-K filings; external validation shows same-industry companies exhibit 63% higher risk profile similarity than cross-industry pairs (Cohen's d=1.06, AUC 0.82, p<0.001), confirming the taxonomy captures economically meaningful structure.
quote: External validation confirms the taxonomy captures economically meaningful structure: same-industry companies exhibit 63% higher risk profile similarity than cross-industry pairs (Cohen's d=1.06, AUC 0.82, p<0.001).
limitations: Validates that the extracted risk labels correlate with industry structure, not that they predict FORWARD RETURNS -- this paper does not itself run a trading/IC test, so it supports the feature's construction validity, not its predictive power (that is exactly what T-17's own IC pilot checks). Abstract/landing page read only, not the full paper PDF, this pass.
independent_replication: Original paper (5 authors); not independently replicated by a third party this pass.
impact_on_spec: Fixes the risk-label feature construction, its data-provenance scope (8-K not 10-K, per local availability), and the mismatched-filing placebo before any IC number is computed in this pilot.

claim: A framework ('LLM as extractor, embedding as ruler') extracts context-aware metric-focused spans from corporate disclosures and quantifies semantic change across consecutive periods via embedding similarity; in portfolio and cross-sectional regression tests against a recent NER-based baseline, this LLM-based method achieves more than twice the risk-adjusted alpha and shows significantly stronger predictive power.
quote: In experiments with portfolio and cross-sectional regression tests against a recent NER-based baseline, our method achieves more than twice the risk-adjusted alpha and shows significantly stronger predictive power.
limitations: Uses earnings-CALL transcripts (metric-tracking across consecutive periods), not 10-K risk factors or 8-K press releases -- a different document type and a different LLM extraction task (metric shift, not risk-label classification) than T-17's actual construction; cited as supporting evidence that LLM-structured disclosure features can add alpha over a baseline, not as a direct replication target. Also, we do not have call-transcript data locally (see negative_experiments_checked) -- this pilot only uses 8-K text.
independent_replication: Original paper; 11-author, multi-institution industry+academia collaboration, not itself a third-party replication of a prior result.
impact_on_spec: Fixes the risk-label feature construction, its data-provenance scope (8-K not 10-K, per local availability), and the mismatched-filing placebo before any IC number is computed in this pilot.

claim: Beginning in 2005 the SEC mandated a 10-K 'risk factor' section; firms facing greater risk disclose more risk factors and allocate disclosure toward the risk types they actually face, and the information conveyed by risk-factor disclosures is reflected in systematic risk, idiosyncratic risk, information asymmetry, and firm value.
quote: Beginning in 2005, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) mandated firms to include a “risk factor” section in their Form 10-K to discuss “the most significant factors that make the company speculative or risky.”
limitations: This is about the 10-K annual Item 1A risk-factor section specifically; T-17's actual local data is 8-K quarterly press releases (EX-99.1), not 10-K Item 1A text -- a different document (see negative_experiments_checked/remaining_evidence_gap for the resulting scope narrowing). Abstract only read (repec.org listing), not the full published article.
independent_replication: Original paper (Review of Accounting Studies 2014); widely cited in accounting/finance literature, not independently re-verified this pass.
impact_on_spec: Fixes the risk-label feature construction, its data-provenance scope (8-K not 10-K, per local availability), and the mismatched-filing placebo before any IC number is computed in this pilot.

claim: Presents explicit formulas for 101 real-life quantitative trading alphas built from cross-sectional rank, time-series, and decay operators; average holding period 0.6-6.4 days; average pairwise alpha correlation 15.9%.
quote:
We present explicit formulas – that are also computer code – for
101 real-life quantitative trading alphas. Their average holding
period approximately ranges 0.6-6.4 days. The average pair-wise
correlation of these alphas is low, 15.9%.
limitations: Contains no LLM, news, or filing-text signal; cited only for the rank/IC evaluation convention.
independent_replication: Widely reused operator library in the public quant-finance literature; not independently re-verified line-by-line this pass.
